findings.lead: Ten statements the figures on the other pages support.  Each is a count, a sum, or a ratio of published numbers, with its basis and a link to the chart behind it.  The page gives no causes, forecasts, or recommendations.  The figures are worked out from the dashboard’s data when the page opens, so they change if a number is corrected.

overview.lead: Colorado’s Orphaned Well Program, run by the Energy and Carbon Management Commission (ECMC), plugs wells and cleans up sites whose operators can’t be found or can’t pay.  This page gathers what ECMC, the Joint Budget Committee, the Interior Department, and other states’ agencies have published about the program’s money, its work, and the wells still on its list, with a link to every source.

cards.title: Program spending by funding source, with wells plugged
cards.lead: Project spending as each ECMC annual report states it.  State fiscal years run July 1 to June 30, so FY26 ended June 30, 2026.  The line shows wells plugged, on the right axis.
notes: The state appropriation came from the Oil and Gas Conservation and Environmental Response Fund, which holds the conservation levy and penalties.  The line item was zeroed after FY24, when enterprise fees took over.
Wells plugged: no FY18 total was found.  FY19 (7) is derived by subtracting FY20 to FY22 from ECMC’s 196 total for FY19 to FY22.

The FY26 report’s text gives a total of $26,524,512.  Its Table 3 lists 93 projects in whole dollars, and those rows sum to $26,524,516, so the $4 difference is rounding.  The chart uses the figures in the text.
FY26 enterprise spending includes $1,182,520 that an operator provided to plug federal wells next to non-federal wells.

cards.title: Orphan inventory: unplugged wells and sites
cards.lead: Counts at the start of each state fiscal year, from the annual reports.  They exclude wells and sites under federal or tribal jurisdiction.  A site can have no well: tank batteries, pits, and flowlines count as sites.
notes: The first count is dated August 1, 2018.  The rest are July 1.
On October 20, 2025, ECMC staff counted 929 wells on 1,906 sites under ECMC jurisdiction and another 393 wells on 523 sites under federal or tribal jurisdiction.

items: Key findings states what the figures show, in ten sentences with their sources.
Funding and spending, Plugging and inventory, and Federal funding hold the charts and tables behind them.
The Unplugged wells pages cover every well on ECMC’s list, one at a time or filtered by county, project, and record.

cards.title: Two counts of the same list
items: The well pages in this dashboard hold every record ECMC’s Orphaned Well Program shapefile marks Unplugged, including wells where the surface or the minerals are Federal, Tribal, or Indian.

ECMC’s annual report counts only wells under its own jurisdiction, so its July 1 figure is smaller than the list file’s.  The Map page’s Federal/Tribal filter shows how many wells on the list fall outside it.
The two counts also carry different dates.  The list file’s retrieval date is in the banner on every well page.

cards.title: Enterprise fee: collected and spent
cards.lead: The Orphan Wells Mitigation Enterprise collects an annual fee on every unplugged well.  ECMC staff gave the board two different sets of collection figures a year apart, so both are shown.  Spending includes administration.
notes: The two presentations agree on FY24 and differ on FY23 (by $125,047) and FY25 (by $1,325,427).  Neither says why.  The September 2026 slide also lists $9,332,300 for FY22, a year before the fee was first charged.
The fund balance was $16,516,144 on June 30, 2025, by the October 2025 presentation.  The June 30, 2026 balance wasn’t found.
FY26 fund spending with administration wasn’t found.  The FY26 annual report gives $6,254,290 of enterprise project spending.

The Joint Budget Committee’s FY2026-27 briefing shows $262,589 spent from the fund in FY24 and $8,378,080 in FY25.  A sentence in the same briefing says the enterprise spent $11.7 million in FY24, which its own table doesn’t support.

cards.title: Sites with work and tasks
notes: A task is one piece of work at a site: plugging, equipment removal, flowline abandonment, sampling, remediation, or reclamation.
A task counts whether it was finished or still in progress at year end, and a task in progress may have started in an earlier year.

FY26 was checked row by row: Table 1 of the annual report lists 1,184 tasks at 813 distinct sites, plus one field-wide task, which matches the report’s text.  Of the 1,184 tasks, 121 are marked Completed and 1,063 In Progress.  Of the 813 sites, 798 are In Progress, 11 Completed, and 4 On Hold.

ECMC’s fee page and its October 2, 2026 news release give 1,035 tasks completed at 807 sites for FY26.  Those figures can’t be reproduced from the annual report’s Table 1.  The chart uses the annual report.

cards.title: Year-over-year change in the well count
cards.lead: ECMC’s annual reports don’t give wells added or removed.  A September 2026 board slide charts wells added by calendar year without printing the values.  Net change is the difference between July 1 counts.  Implied additions add back the wells plugged that year, so they’re approximate.  For FY26, SRA counts 14 plugged wells with federal or tribal surface or minerals in ECMC’s records, and the July 1 lists exclude such wells.  Leaving them out gives about 195 for that year in place of 209.  The count matches Table 1 of the annual report to ECMC’s ownership fields.  Table 1 shows 164 sites with a well plugged against the report’s 161, so the 14 could be off by one or two.

cols.label: Implied wells added in the year just ended

notes: CPR News reported 576 wells added in FY24, of which Omimex Petroleum (339) and WME Yates (212) were 96%.  The derived figure for that year is 606.
Wells also leave the list when ECMC finds a responsible party or corrects a record.  ECMC doesn’t publish those removals, so the implied additions run low by however many there were.

cards.title: What’s pending

items.t: Potential claims covering 1,215 wells were noticed, set for hearing, or in pre-hearing negotiation, 1,054 of them from one operator.  ECMC’s slides don’t name the operator.
The Colorado Sun identifies the operator as K.P. Kauffman Company and gives 1,041 wells.

ECMC staff filed an enforcement application against K.P. Kauffman Company Inc. on July 23, 2026, as Cause 1V, Docket 260700198.  It asks the Commission to find violations and assess a penalty, and to have the Director foreclose the operator’s financial assurance if the operator doesn’t pay or return to compliance within 35 days of an order.  It also asks the Commission to authorize, but not require, the Director to declare the operator’s wells orphaned.  Exhibit A to a staff motion of September 1 lists 1,575 wells with the company as operator of record, from a facility search dated July 13, 2026.  Of those, 1,164 carry a facility status other than PA or AL, read here as plugged and abandoned and as abandoned location, and 1,055 of the 1,164 have fee or state minerals (derived).  No filing read gives the 1,054 figure or says how it was counted.  The docket showed no order and no filing after September 22 when checked on November 19, 2026.
On June 4, 2026 the court affirmed a $1,935,030 penalty and a suspension order against that operator in an unpublished opinion.
Approved orders covered 71 fee or state wells likely to be added in calendar 2026.
Staff reported sampling or methane monitoring at 548 sites, reclamation at 156 sites, weed management at more than 300 others, and 284 facilities decommissioned.

Staff told the board the program mitigated about 1,371 metric tons of methane a year from July 2022 through June 2026.  A footnote on the same slide gives a four-year cumulative total of 3,300 metric tons, which is the figure in the annual report.

cards.title: Federal actions since 2025 that bear on Colorado

items.t: Interior’s revised formula grant guidance made methane measurement before and after plugging optional unless state law requires it, and dropped the post-award environmental review.

ECMC revised its Phase 2 and Matching applications to the new guidance on July 25, 2025, and they were still pending on October 21, 2025.  No Colorado-specific freeze amount or release date was found.
ECMC reported that a new endangered species and historic preservation screening delayed projects by several months each in FY25.
Interior’s FY2026 report says Public Law 119-74 moved $285 million of unobligated orphaned well money to wildland fire.  The law itself wasn’t read for this page.

BLM’s 2024 rule raised minimum bonds to $150,000 per lease and $500,000 statewide.  In December 2025 BLM moved the statewide compliance date to June 22, 2027, and in June 2026 it proposed returning to the earlier minimums.  No final rule was found.
Interior reports wells plugged by bureau for the nation only, so there’s no published count for BLM, Forest Service, or Park Service land in Colorado.

No Colorado count of wells measured before and after plugging was found in Interior’s reports.  ECMC’s FY26 report says plugging orphaned wells eliminated a cumulative total of more than 3,330 metric tons of atmospheric methane from July 2022 through June 2026.

states.lead: Where Colorado sits beside other oil and gas states on published figures.  States define an orphaned well differently, count different costs, and report on different calendars, so each chart states its basis.  The page reports positions on each measure and doesn’t grade them.

policy.lead: How Colorado’s financial assurance rules, dedicated fees, idle-well rules, and definitions sit beside other states’, as in force in November 2026. cards.title: Colorado’s 2022 financial assurance rules in brief

items.t: Each operator files a financial assurance plan under one of six options tied to its well count and production.

The option follows the operator’s average daily production per well: Option 1 above 60 barrels of oil equivalent, Option 2 above 15 and up to 60, Option 3 above 2 and up to 15, and Option 4 for everyone else, including operators reporting no production.  Option 5 is for individual circumstances and Option 6 for larger public and private companies.

The blanket covers low-producing wells up to 10% of an operator’s wells under Option 1 and 5% under Option 2.  Wells past that share, and low-producing wells that change hands, need single-well financial assurance.
Single-well financial assurance for every well, paid in over time: a presumptive 5% of the total each year under Option 3 and 10% under Option 4.

Either the operator’s demonstrated cost, or the commission’s estimates: $10,000 to plug a well of 4,000 feet or less, $30,000 for 4,000 to 8,000 feet, and $40,000 beyond 8,000 feet, plus the well’s share of $100,000 of reclamation per location.
COGCC’s fact sheet said the rules raise amounts 10 to 30 times for mid and high production operators and likely put single-well assurance on over half the state’s wells.
A 2018 legislative attachment cites $20,000 per well for plugging and inactive wells as the requirement then.
ECMC’s current rule set still links the April 30, 2022 text of the 700 Series.

cards.title: Changes in other states, 2025 and 2026

items.t: An Oil Conservation Commission rule effective September 22, 2026 sets $150,000 one-well assurance or a $250,000 blanket for active wells.  An industry group has said it’s weighing a legal challenge.
A tiered, risk-based bonding rule took effect July 8, 2026.
SB 1150 limits extensions for wells inactive 15 or more years and at least 25 years old from September 1, 2027.  The Railroad Commission proposed implementing rules in October 2026.
HB 1369 began phasing in tiered surety on November 1, 2025.
Idle well fees now run $1,000 to $22,500 per well per year, with $60,000 for wells idle 25 or more years from 2029.

Definitions, including Orphaned Well, Orphaned Site, and Out of Service Well.

Plugging, inactive wells, and out of service wells, in the 400 Series.
The federal orphaned well program.  On state and private land, a state’s own definition of orphaned well governs.

defs.t: C.R.S. 34-60-133(8)(f) uses one term, orphaned well, for a well, location, or facility with no owner or operator that can be found, or whose owner or operator is unwilling or unable to pay for plugging, reclaiming, and remediating it.

The 100 Series keeps two terms.  An Orphaned Well has no owner or operator that can be found, or one unwilling or unable to plug it.  An Orphaned Site is a location or facility with no operator holding unclaimed financial assurance or an active registration and no responsible party identified by the commission.  A site may have no well.
Added to the statute in 2024: an oil and gas well with a high risk of becoming orphaned.

Executive Order D 2018-012 defined an Orphaned Well the way today’s rule does, and an Orphaned Site by environmental impact: a site where oil and gas operations have caused or may cause a significant adverse environmental impact and no responsible party can be found or is willing or able to mitigate it.
The commission rewrote Orphaned Site as a status test.  Its stated reason was that the program also reclaims and remediates sites with no well or an already plugged well.

items.title: 2027 orphan well mitigation fee
items.summary: Raised the annual fee from $225 and $125 to $285 and $155 per well, effective April 2027.  The marginal well fee stays $115.  ECMC expects about $10.7 million in 2027.  From 2028 the fee adjusts each year by the consumer price index for energy commodities.

items.title: BLM Oil and Gas Leasing, proposed rule
items.summary: Would return federal minimum bond amounts to their pre-2024 levels.  Comments closed August 24, 2026.  No final rule was found.

items.title: Kauffman v. Oil and Gas Conservation Commission
items.summary: The Court of Appeals, in an unpublished opinion, affirmed a $1,935,030 penalty and a suspension order against an operator with about 1,200 wells.

items.title: Development of Thermal Energy Resources
items.summary: ECMC and the Colorado Geological Survey gather subsurface data for geothermal development, reported to include voluntary data from orphaned and marginal wells.  A report was due November 15, 2026.

items.title: Technical Changes to Energy and Carbon Management Statutes
items.summary: Terminology changes in Article 60.  No change to orphaned well funding.

items.title: Transfer from IIJA orphaned wells balances
items.summary: By Interior’s account, moved $285 million of unobligated orphaned well money to wildland fire, lowering the national program total to $4.392 billion.  The law itself wasn’t read.

items.title: BLM statewide bond phase-in extension
items.summary: Moved the compliance date for statewide federal bonds from June 22, 2026 to June 22, 2027.

items.title: Oil and Gas Reporting: Production, Emissions, and Severance Taxes
items.summary: A State Auditor performance audit of operator reporting across ECMC, CDPHE, and the Department of Revenue.  It isn’t specific to orphaned wells, and no audit of the orphaned well program was found.

items.title: Revised State Formula Grant Guidance
items.summary: Replaced the 2023 and 2024 formula grant guidance.  Methane measurement became optional unless state law requires it.

items.title: Enterprise Marginal Well Plugging program parameters
items.summary: Set which operators and wells qualify for reimbursement of marginal well plugging.

items.title: Geologic Storage Enterprise and Geothermal Resources
items.summary: Created a separate stewardship enterprise that can fund orphaned geologic storage facilities.  It doesn’t change the oil and gas orphan enterprise.  The signing date wasn’t confirmed.

items.title: Marginal well mitigation fee
items.summary: A new flat fee of $115 per well per year from April 2025, forecast to raise $5 million a year.  The orphan fee didn’t change.

items.title: Energy and Carbon Management Regulation
items.summary: No direct orphaned well provision.  Extended the period for bringing a violation to three years after discovery.

items.title: Oil and Gas Production Fees
items.summary: No orphaned well provision.  Production fees fund transit and wildlife and land remediation from July 1, 2025.

items.title: Ozone Mitigation Measures
items.summary: Let the enterprise pay for plugging marginal wells and defined "marginal well" in statute.  Added grounds for suspending or revoking an operator’s license.

items.title: BLM Fluid Mineral Leases and Leasing Process rule
items.summary: Raised federal minimum bonds to $150,000 per lease and $500,000 statewide, effective June 22, 2024.

items.title: Mod to Energy and Carbon Management Processes
items.summary: Would have made prior owners and operators jointly and severally responsible for mitigation costs, and ended new permits by 2030.  Postponed indefinitely.

items.title: Energy and Carbon Management Regulation in Colorado
items.summary: Renamed the Colorado Oil and Gas Conservation Commission the Energy and Carbon Management Commission, and the response fund the Energy and Carbon Management Cash Fund, effective July 1, 2023.

items.title: Orphan Well Mitigation Fee Rulemaking
items.summary: Aligned Rule 205 with SB 22-198 and set the production threshold between the two fee tiers at 15 barrels of oil equivalent or 22 thousand cubic feet equivalent a day.  The rulemaking record gives July 30, 2022 as the effective date and ECMC’s press release gives August 1.

items.title: Orphaned Oil and Gas Wells Enterprise
items.summary: Created the Orphaned Wells Mitigation Enterprise, its board, and its cash fund, with per-well fees of $125 and $225, effective July 1, 2022.  The fiscal note estimated $10.4 million a year.

items.title: Financial Assurance Rulemaking
items.summary: Operator-specific financial assurance plans in six options tied to production, single-well assurance for low producers, transfer and out of service requirements, and a pooled orphan fee.  Effective April 30, 2022.

items.title: Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act: orphaned well site plugging, remediation, and restoration
items.summary: $4.275 billion for state grants.  A state’s own definition of orphaned well governs on state and private land.  Colorado’s awards total about $89.9 million.

items.title: Mission change rules
items.summary: Reorganized the rule set after SB 19-181.  The 1000 Series reclamation rules in force today carry this date.

items.title: Oil and Gas Operator Financial Assurance
items.summary: Would have required at least $270,000 of financial assurance per well.  The title was set and a rehearing denied on February 19, 2020.  It didn’t reach the ballot.

items.title: Protect Public Welfare Oil and Gas Operations
items.summary: Required rules making every operator show financial capability, with a pooled orphan fund to be considered, and changed the fund balance cap.  The fiscal note showed $3.0 million of revenue, about $0.96 million of cost, and 7.0 FTE.

items.title: Orphaned wells and sites
items.summary: Required a prioritized list by August 1, 2018, annual reports, a July 1, 2023 target for medium and high priority wells, a working group report by December 1, 2018, and financial assurance rules by September 1, 2019.  The order’s text is reproduced as a scanned attachment in the Joint Budget Committee’s FY2019-20 hearing document.  The link to the order on the old COGCC site no longer works.
links: Order text, in the JBC hearing document

items.title: Orphaned Well Program appropriation
items.summary: Raised the program’s line from $445,000 to $5,011,000 with two-year spending authority.  The bill number wasn’t confirmed.

items.title: Roll Over Year-end Balance Environmental Response Account
items.summary: The year-end balance of the environmental response account stays in the account.  The fiscal note showed no fiscal impact.

items.title: Oil and gas penalty authority
items.summary: Set the current ceiling of $15,000 per violation per day.  Penalties flow to the environmental response account.  The legislature’s bill page no longer loads, so this rests on the statute’s history note and ECMC’s 2014 rulemaking page.

items.title: First orphan well plugging appropriation
items.summary: First budget authority to plug historic wells with no financial assurance, paid from the levy and penalties.  The line ran through FY24.  The bill number wasn’t found.

gaps: ECMC’s annual reports don’t give wells added to or removed from the orphan list each year, or annual totals of sites closed.  A September 2026 board slide charts sites and wells added by calendar year without printing the values.
ECMC doesn’t publish a current average cost to plug a well or close a site.  The only published averages are for 2012 to 2017.
No official time series of total financial assurance held, or of assurance against estimated liability, was found.
Wells plugged with federal money, as distinct from the program total, aren’t published.
ECMC’s two board presentations give different fee collections for FY23 and FY25, and neither explains the difference.  The enterprise fund balance on June 30, 2026 wasn’t found.

ECMC’s fee page and news release give 1,035 tasks completed at 807 sites for FY26.  The annual report’s Table 1 lists 1,184 tasks at 813 sites, 121 of them marked Completed, and the two can’t be reconciled from the published documents.
Wells plugged before FY19 weren’t found as annual totals.
No Colorado State Auditor report on the orphaned well program or on financial assurance was found.
IOGCC’s 2026 state-by-state orphan counts weren’t available, so cross-state inventory figures are as of December 2023.
No published comparison explains why Colorado’s spending per well differs from other states’.
Interior doesn’t publish wells plugged on federal land by state.
